I. INTRODUCTION
The City of San Gabriel (“City”) is requesting proposals from qualified consultants (Consultant) that
meet the Secretary of the Interior’s Professional Qualification Standards for historian and/or
architectural historian to prepare a Historic Resources Survey (HRS) for the City of San Gabriel as
a whole. The Consultant must have extensive experience completing survey work. The Consultant
will prepare a historic resources survey and local historic district study report as part of this
contract. This would be the City’s first-ever comprehensive program to identify significant historic
resources throughout the city.

A citywide historic resources survey serves as a tool for identifying, recording, and evaluating
cultural resources, including buildings, structures, objects, sites, historic districts, planning
features, public art and parks, cultural landscapes, and other features within the City of San
Gabriel. A historic resources survey is a process of systematically identifying and recording
information on properties and neighborhoods that reflect the City’s architectural, social, and
cultural history. Field surveys are to cover the entire City of San Gabriel in an area of 4.1 square
miles.

The survey data will provide baseline information on potential historic resources to guide long-
range planning decisions, inform project review, and support City policy goals. As part of the
process, the survey will gather various types of information on potential historic resources
including construction and ownership history, architectural styles, reasons for significance,
relevant evaluation criteria, and photographs. The survey will include a survey report and
appendices summarizing survey findings by resource type as listed in subsection III. The survey
will explain the tools and methodology used to conduct the field surveys and outline the resource
evaluation and documentation process.

The survey will identify and evaluate properties according to standardized criteria for listing in the
National Register of Historic Places (National Register), California Register of Historical Resources
(California Register), and for local designation as City Historic-Cultural Landmarks and Historic
Districts per San Gabriel Municipal Code (SGMC) § 153.606 through § 153.613. The survey will be
conducted from the public-right-of-way. All properties that are surveyed will be assigned a
California Historic Resources (CHR) Code, and only properties that appear to meet criteria for
listing will be recorded on State of California Department of Parks and Recreation (DPR) forms.
The survey findings are subject to updates over time as properties age, additional information is
uncovered, and more detailed research and analyses are completed. Resources identified through
the survey are not automatically designated resources. Designation by the City of San Gabriel and
nominations to the California or National Registers are separate processes, which include property
owner notification and public hearings.

Under the direction of the City’s Director of Community Development, the consultant will provide
the range of expertise necessary to carry out the survey. The successful consultant shall also have
the resources to provide cost effective and timely services, including providing outstanding
   City of San Gabriel
  Request for Proposals – Historic Resources Survey
  Page 3

customer service to the City and its related clients. All work shall be performed and deliverables
produced in accordance with guidance and bulletins from the National Park Service (NPS) and the
State Office of Historic Preservation (OHP).

This project will be a joint effort led by the selected consultant team, City staff, the Historic
Preservation and Cultural Resources Commission, the San Gabriel City Council, and the
preservation community and will include participating in community outreach and public hearings
to discuss survey results and take questions from the Commission, City Council, and public. It is
vital that the consultant meets all of the required deadlines, which are outlined in the "Anticipated
Schedule for RFP" section of this RFP. The City anticipates the process to take approximately
twelve months. The City plans to enter into an agreement with the selected consulting firm based
on negotiated scope of work and proposed fee. The scope and fee do not include any CEQA
analysis or any CEQA work that may be required as part of this project.

I.  CURRENT HISTORIC PRESERVATION POLICY AND EFFORTS

San Gabriel first established itself as a leader in historic preservation in 1965, when it became only
the second city in the county, following Los Angeles, to adopt a historic preservation ordinance.
During the ensuing half-century, the City has designated and protected local landmarks and
completed historic resource surveys for four portions of the city, ranging from the Mission District
to commercial architecture along Valley Boulevard.

San Gabriel offers preservation incentives alongside its preservation protections, including the
popular Mills Act property tax abatement program and fee reductions for qualified historic
preservation projects. To foster and recognize local efforts in historic preservation, San Gabriel
offers the annual Martin E. Weil Award to honor notable preservation projects, organizations, or
individuals.

The City of San Gabriel has a partner in its preservation efforts with the San Gabriel Historical
Association (SGHA). In 1976, the committee formed to celebrate the nation’s bicentennial became
the historical committee and the San Gabriel Historical Association was the result. More
information about the SGHA can be found on their website: https://www.sghistorical.org/.

The Los Angeles Conservancy, a non-profit advocacy and education organization, published their
second edition of a “preservation report card” in March 2014. The report card grades each of the
88 cities within Los Angeles County on their historic preservation programs. San Gabriel received
a B grade. https://www.laconservancy.org/resources/report-card/report. We anticipate the
grade to rise in the future, as the City begins to implement or fulfill key aspects of its expanded
historic preservation program.

General Plan Policy

The City’s General Plan includes a Cultural Resources chapter with the following Goals and Targets
regarding historic preservation:
   City of San Gabriel
  Request for Proposals – Historic Resources Survey
  Page 4

GOAL 11.1: Preserve and protect valuable but threatened resources.

Target 11.1.1: Preserve existing historically significant structures, i.e., pre- and post-statehood
artifacts, adobes, Mission-era outbuildings and structures.

Target 11.1.3: Use the principles and practices of land use planning, historic preservation,
archaeology, art history, anthropology and history to promote preservation and adaptive reuse of
cultural resources.

GOAL 11.2: Celebrate San Gabriel’s connection to the culture of the Tongva People.

Target 11.2.3: Inventory structures, paleontological sites, archaeological sites, cultural landscapes,
artifacts and documents in San Gabriel and institutions associated with the Tongva/Gabrielino
people.

GOAL 11.6: Need to conserve and protect.

Target 11.6.1: Foster a neighborhood conservation ethic.

Target 11.6.2: Ensure that other community policies and plans should complement community
conservation goals.

GOAL 11.7: Create a database documenting the breadth and wealth of San Gabriel’s cultural
resources.

Target 11.7.1: Document and recognize buildings and structures that have historic value.

Target 11.7.3: Partner with community organizations such as the San Gabriel Historical
Association, California Preservation Foundation, Los Angeles Conservancy and Pasadena Heritage.

GOAL 11.9: Preserve and protect our cultural landscapes from damage and degradation.

Target 11.9.1: Protect and preserve bridges and other engineering features of merit.

Target 11.9.2: Protect and preserve historic and cultural landscapes.

Certified Local Government (CLG)

On December 3, 2019, City Council authorized Planning Division staff to file a Certified Local
Government (CLG) application with the State Office of Historic Preservation (OHP). The National
Historic Preservation Act of 1966, provided for the establishment of a CLG program to encourage
the direct participation of local governments in the identification, evaluation, registration, and
preservation of historic properties within their jurisdictions. The CLG program is a partnership
among local governments, OHP, and the National Park Service (NPS), which is responsible for
administering the National Historic Preservation Program. The benefits of becoming a CLG include
   City of San Gabriel
  Request for Proposals – Historic Resources Survey
  Page 5

possible grant funding for preservation related efforts, technical assistance from OHP, and
credibility that the San Gabriel Historic Preservation and Cultural Resource Ordinance is consistent
with federal and state standards.

On August 19, 2021, OHP provided review comments regarding the application. Staff reviewed
the recommended changes suggested by the OHP and updated the City’s Historic Preservation
Ordinance so the CLG application could be resubmitted back to OHP for review before the end of
this year. On December 20, 2021, OHP submitted the CLG application to NPS with an approval
recommendation. The goal is to get certified by April 2022 so the City would be eligible to compete
for grant funding opportunities in 2022.

Previous Surveys

Over the course of the last two decades, work on six historic resource surveys has been done. This
represents a review of close to 700 properties in the City. None of the surveys, however, met the
requirements for an historical resource survey as contained in Section 5024.1(g) of the California
Government Code. In 2003, during the preparation of the Valley Boulevard Specific Plan,
preservation architect Martin Weil did a windshield survey of neighborhoods in the plan area.
Similarly, he completed one in 2004 which became part of the Mission District Specific Plan. The
2004 General Plan also contained a map showing historic and cultural resources. Finally, in 2006,
a team of students from Cal Poly Pomona, led by Professor Anna Maria Whitaker, surveyed four
residential neighborhoods: Northwest San Gabriel, the Country Club, San Gabriel Village and the
area south of Valley Boulevard. The State Department of Parks and Recreation (DPR) forms were
created by the students as part of this process. Although, not all the DPR forms were verified, the
database complied through this process provides a good baseline of information for these
neighborhoods. The data from previous surveys is available in a spreadsheet format as well as
electronic copies of the draft DPR forms from the 2006 survey.

Demolition and Neighborhood Compatibility

On October 6, 2015, the City Council adopted Urgency Ordinance No. 621-C.S. placing a
moratorium on the demolition of single-family homes and the development of new second stories
in the R-1 (Single-Family Residence) zone to protect the City’s older neighborhoods, address
mansionization concerns and put new policies regarding demolition and replacement projects in
place. On October 3, 2017, City Council approved Urgency Ordinance No. 639-C.S., adopting new
development standards for properties in the R-1 zone and a new review process for development
in the R-1 zone. New second stories are processed as SPRs and require City Architect review before
Design Review Commission (DRC) consideration.

III.  PROJECT NEED

Local Setting and Regulatory Framework
As a Mission City with strong Spanish influences combined with a historic downtown and
surrounding residential neighborhoods developed in the early 1900’s, the City of San Gabriel is
rich in historic resources that span a substantial timeframe. Other influences in the City’s
development pattern, such as development before and after WWII, have not been fully described
or explored. In particular, the City needs to be assured that historic resources surveys are
consistent with guidance and bulletins from the NPS and OHP.

San Gabriel’s Historic Preservation and Cultural Resources Ordinance dates to 1965, when it
became only the second such ordinance to be adopted in Los Angeles County. The ordinance was
comprehensively updated in 2017 and a Historic Preservation and Cultural Resources Commission
(HPCRC) was created.
   City of San Gabriel
  Request for Proposals – Historic Resources Survey
  Page 7

The HPCRC identified the need for a historic context statement and historic resources survey as
priorities. With a formal adopted Historic Context Statement, the City is now better equipped to
assist the citizens of San Gabriel and developers by providing a greater level of consistency
regarding identification and classification of historic resources. The City is in a better position to
identify and preserve its historic resources, as well as to forward its own preservation policies and
objectives. The Historic Context Statement has strengthened the tools available for the
identification, management, protection, and interpretation of historic resources.

Relationship between Historic Context Statement and Historic Resources Survey

On October 5, 2021, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 21-41 approving the City of San
Gabriel Historic Context Statement. One of the most important components of the Historic
Context Statement is the establishment of a multiple-property framework for identifying and
evaluating individual resources and potential historic districts. The Historic Context Statement
serves to facilitate the evaluation of individual properties by comparing them with resources that
share similar physical characteristics and historical associations throughout the City. The Historic
Context Statement explains the associated property types, period of significance, evaluation
criteria, integrity thresholds, and registration requirements for properties qualifying under each
significant contextual theme.

The Historic Context Statement framework is to be used as the basis for developing a survey. The
survey is to focus on identifying resources dating from about 1770 to 1980. Properties may be
significant under more than one context and theme and may be evaluated under each that applies.
For example, a commercial building may be significant for its architectural qualities as well as for
the long-time occupant that may have been an important business in the commercial history of a
community.

In addition to addressing patterns of development and historic associations of the built
environment from the 1770s to the 1980s, the Historic Context Statement includes an
Architecture and Design Context that thematically groups architectural styles and includes
descriptions of associated property types and subtypes and their registration requirements,
significant architectural attributes and styles, character-defining features, registration
requirements, and integrity thresholds.

The Historic Context Statement will aid in the identification of the City's historic resources in a way
that is consistent with State and Federal standards. The content and user-friendliness of the
Historic Context Statement will assure that the public has access to a complete understanding of
the framework used to identify the City's historic resources. Together with the context, the survey
will give property owners and business people the information they need to better understand
which alterations are considered acceptable (based on its connection within context) and will help
the HPCRC evaluate proposals for alterations to properties considered historic resources.

The survey will identify, record, and evaluate resources based on the established periods of
historical significance, important associated property types, and character-defining and
   City of San Gabriel
  Request for Proposals – Historic Resources Survey
  Page 8

associative features for each of the important themes as outlined in the Historic Context
Statement. The survey will utilize established evaluation criteria and integrity thresholds for
identifying and evaluating individual resources and historic districts for the National, California,
and local registration programs. The survey can also include the identification and documentation
of additional contexts, themes, or subthemes not identified at the time of the context.

Although the field surveyor will cover the entire City, only resources that have been identified as
significant within the contexts developed in the Historic Context Statement are to be fully
recorded. Resources not recorded may require additional research and analysis as part of project
review and compliance with state and federal environmental review processes associated with
development projects. Properties that are not visible from the street are typically not recorded;
some may be flagged for additional research if there is known information at the time of the
survey (for example the work of a particular architect, but property integrity cannot be assessed
due to visibility issues).

The survey will evaluate the contribution of individual structures to a potential historic district or
thematic grouping. All survey work will meet NPS and OHP standards. Each surveyed property or
group of properties will be evaluated and categorized by context(s) and theme(s), as appropriate.
Evaluation will be based on National Register, California Register and local criteria.

The survey will address how to use the document for the public's understanding, for
Commissioner's use, and future surveyors, provide an explanation about how to apply the
National Register Criteria for Evaluation, include user-friendly format with tables, bulleted lists,
graphics, and other illustrations as appropriate, explain how to address properties that may be
significant under more than one context, and provide recommendations for future study, context
development, or survey work.

Resource Types

The survey is to identify individual resources, non-parcel resources, potential historic districts, and
district contributors and non-contributors. Each of these is described below.

  •  Individual Resources are generally resources located within a single assessor parcel
  such as a residence or duplex. However, a parcel may include more than one individual
  resource, if each appears to be significant.

  •  Non-Parcel Resources are not associated with Assessor Parcel Numbers (APNs) and
  generally do not have addresses. Examples may include street trees, street lamps,
  landscaped medians, bridges, and signs.

  •  Historic Districts are areas that are related geographically and by theme. Districts may
  include single or multiple parcels depending on the resource. Examples of resources
  that may be recorded as historic districts include residential neighborhoods, garden
  apartments, commercial areas, large estates, school and hospital campuses, and
  industrial complexes.

  historic districts. Non-contributing resources may be those that are extensively altered,
  built recently, or that do not relate to historic contexts and themes defined for the

III. DESCRIPTION OF THE CITY
A. The City of San Gabriel

  San Gabriel is located approximately 10 miles northeast of the City of Los Angeles and was
  incorporated in 1913 as a general law city which operates under the council-manager form
  of government. The City Council is comprised of five members who are elected at large
  serving a staggered term of four years. The City provides a full range of municipal services
  including police and fire protection, engineering and planning, street maintenance, traffic
  control, code enforcement, parks and recreation services, and general administrative
  activities. Today, San Gabriel is an ethnically and socio-economically diverse city. It is a built-
  out community and, as a result, new development is almost entirely adaptive reuse,
  intensification, and replacement. It has not experienced significant population growth since
  the 1990s, a decade during which the City grew by 7.3 percent and added nearly 2,700 new
  residents. During the 2000s, San Gabriel’s population increased by only 0.3 percent. The City
  encompasses 4.1 square miles with a population of 41,255 and is developed with a mix of
  residential and commercial uses, as well as limited institutional, industrial and parkland uses.

  For a small city, San Gabriel has long played an outsized role in the history of Southern
  California. Known as the “Birthplace of the L.A. Region”, San Gabriel was the starting point
  for 44 settlers or “pobladores” who walked nine miles west and founded the city of Los
  Angeles. San Gabriel first demonstrated its commitment to preserving its history with the
  adoption of a historic preservation ordinance in 1965, only the second city in Los Angeles
  County to do so. This ordinance was completely updated and expanded in 2017 and is
  supplemented by a Cultural Resources chapter in the City’s General Plan.

IV. SCOPE OF SERVICES REQUESTED:
SCOPE OF SERVICES TO BE PERFORMED

The City of San Gabriel is seeking proposals from qualified consulting firms to prepare a
comprehensive Citywide Historic Resources Survey consistent with the themes identified in the
City’s Historic Context Statement. Work will commence on April 25, 2022 and end on April 29,
2023. Adopting the Citywide HRS will be a joint effort of the selected consultant team, City staff,
the Historic Preservation and Cultural Resource Commission, the City Council and interested
citizens and stakeholders. The consultant will be required to work closely with the Commission
and members of the Planning staff. The results of the project will be presented to the Historic
Preservation and Cultural Resource Commission and City Council. The proposal should include a
conceptual timeline for the completion of this project that addresses all the components in the
Scope of Work.

The activities/tasks for the consultant would include the following:
  1. Review the San Gabriel Historic Context and existing surveys and plans;

  2. Research other existing City documents and available primary and secondary
  resources to help build the background for the resources survey;

  3. Conduct a field survey of the project area;

  4. Locate, identify, photograph, and provide an inventory form for historic buildings,
  structures, objects, and sites which may be eligible for designation as a historic
  landmark or as a contributing resource to a historic district;

  5. Provide information to assist with a webpage on the City’s website to describe activity
  and invite public comments;
   City of San Gabriel
  Request for Proposals – Historic Resources Survey
  Page 14

  6. Consult with the San Gabriel Historical Association, neighborhood groups, and other
  interested citizens groups and professionals to gather information and build
  awareness and consensus for project approach and objectives;

  7. Conduct two (2) to three (3) public workshops to engage interested citizens,
  neighborhood groups and local professionals from the development and preservation
  community;

  8. Attend as many "working" meetings with staff as necessary in performing work scope
  tasks;

  9. Prepare a project outline and bibliography;

  10. Prepare draft Historic Resource Survey and distribute to City staff;

  11. Attend four (4) public meetings of the Historic Preservation and Cultural Resources
  Commission, and one (1) City Council meeting to answer questions as the HRS moves
  through the approval process; and

  12. Incorporate comments from City staff; prepare final Historic Resource Survey.

POLICY DOCUMENTS

The selected consultant will meet with City staff to establish project goals and objectives and
confirm the project schedule. Using the City’s existing lists of potential and designated historic
resources, General Plan policies, current historic preservation ordinance, demolition and
neighborhood compatibility ordinances, Historic Context Statement, data from previous
incomplete survey projects, and information provided by local historians as the starting point, the
consultant shall prepare a historic resources survey.

All work shall be performed, and deliverables produced, in accordance with National Register
Bulletin 24 Guidelines for Local Surveys: A Basis for Preservation Planning and the Secretary of the
Interior’s Standards for Identification and Evaluation. The consultant shall meet the Secretary of
the Interior’s Professional Qualifications for historian and architectural historian as set forth in 36
CFR Part 61, Appendix A. The historic resources survey will need to be consistent with standards
and guidelines established by NPS and OHP. The effort will result in a document containing a
complete historic resources survey to identify significant resources associated with each theme
and period outlined in the Historic Context Statement.

The resulting document should include a discussion of how the survey findings will be
incorporated into local planning as well as identify potential “next steps”. The survey will help
determine appropriate resources that will need to be allocated in the future.

OUTREACH AND TRAINING
Public outreach is integral to a successful historic preservation program. In San Gabriel we utilize
newsletters, newspaper ads, mailers, public workshops within neighborhoods, web pages, social
media, and last but not least, noticed public hearings as part of our outreach efforts. Since
longtime San Gabriel residents are often helpful in identifying local history, we hope to engage
residents as we begin to formulate a draft historic resources survey. The City and consultant will
work with, neighborhood groups, and local professionals to ensure that the survey is guided by a
broad spectrum of local knowledge. The final product will be available on the City’s website,
available as a document at the City, the public library, and given as resource materials to all City
decision makers.

The selected consultant is responsible for recommending an outreach program as part of the work
scope. This step is imperative to ensure that the survey’s approach and process is inclusive. The
program should facilitate public input to engage interested parties including members of the
public, property owners, the Spanish‐speaking community, the Chinese‐speaking community,
community stakeholders (SGHA and others), City staff, Commissioners (Historic Preservation and
Cultural Resources), and City Council.

The selected consultant will provide training for Planning staff and the Historic Preservation and
Cultural Resources Commission on how to utilize the survey in future policy development and
during project review.

CITY OF SAN GABRIEL
  MINUTES OF THE HISTORIC PRESERVATION AND CULTURAL RESOURCE
  COMMISSION SPECIAL MEETING
  WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 16, 2022

  CALL TO ORDER

  The Historic Preservation and Cultural Resource Commission special meeting
  was called to order 6:31 p.m. on February 16, 2022.

  PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE

  The Pledge of Allegiance was led by Commissioner Urena.

  ROLL CALL – COMMISSION

  Present: Chair Lubisich,  Vice-Chair  Mojarro,  Commissioner  Urena,  and
  Commissioner Weeks.

  Excused: Commissioner DeVriednt

  Staff in attendance included Planning Manager Tewasart, Senior Planner Chang
  and Historic Preservation and Cultural Resource Commission Secretary Ortiz.

1.  PUBLIC COMMENT

  None.

2.  APPROVAL OF MINUTES

  Minutes from the August 25, 2021 HPCRC meeting.

  Commissioner Urena moved to approve the minutes from the August 25, 2021
  HPCRC meeting. Commissioner Weeks seconded the motion. Motion passed by
  a vote of 4 ayes, 0 noes.

3.  SECRETARY OF INTERIOR STANDARD TRAINING

  City Architectural Historian to provide training on Secretary of Interior’s Standards.

  This item was presented by Jen Mermilliod, City Architectural Historian.

  Vice-Chair Mojarro thanked Jen Mermilliod for the presentation.
   Chair Lubisich requested if they can be walked through a case study for a future
  training.

  Chair Lubisich opened the public hearing.

  There being no speaker, Chair Lubisich closed the public hearing.

4.  DRAFT HISTORIC RESOURCES SURVEY REQUEST FOR PROPOSAL (RFP)

  This item is to provide an update regarding the Historic Resources Survey request
  for proposal (RFP).

  This item was presented by Planning Manager Tewasart.

  Chair Lubisich asked if there was access to the student survey that was performed.
  She also asked if the amount allotted was enough to do a City survey.

  Chair Lubisich opened the public hearing.

  There being no speaker, Chair Lubisich closed the public hearing.

5.  LAND ACKNOWLEDGEMENT STATEMENT UPDATE

  On August 17, 2021, the City Council formed a Land Acknowledgement Statement
  (LAS) Advisory Committee comprised of two members from the HPCRC and
  HEAR Commissions. On September 14, 2021, the Committee held its first meeting
  to discuss the purpose of the Committee and develop an action plan. On October
  6, 2021, the Committee held a second meeting to review a purpose statement and
  finalize a questionnaire to tribal leaders. On November 10, 2021, the Committee
  held discussions with Chief Redblood Anthony Morales of the Gabrieleno San
  Gabriel Band of Mission Indians and Chieftain Andrew Salas of the Gabrieleno
  Band of Mission Indians Kizh Nation.

  This item was presented by Chair Lubisich.

  Chair Lubisich provided the Commission with an update.

  Chair Lubisich opened the public hearing.

  There being no speaker, Chair Lubisich closed the public hearing.

6.  CERTIFIED LOCAL GOVERNMENT (CLG) APPLICATION UPDATE

   This item is to provide an update regarding the Certified Local Government (CLG)
  application.

  This item was presented by Jen Mermilliod.

  Jen Mermilliod stated the revised CLG application was reviewed and a package
  was put together for the CLG application to the National Park Service. Comments
  from the National Park Service were received which need to be addressed.

  Chair Lubisich opened the public hearing.

  There being no speaker, Chair Lubisich closed the public hearing.

7.  STAFF ITEMS

  Planning Manager Tewasart informed the Commission about the Homeless Count
  and indicated that volunteers are still needed.

8.  COMMISSIONER COMMENTS AND CONFERENCE/MEETING REPORTS

  Chair Lubisich stated she attended the California Preservation Foundation in
  December. She also inquired about the Bell Awards. She also requested if Staff
  could update the Commission in between meetings with items that are
  preservation related.
